newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Interpol to aid Georgia in battle against crime.
newsitem.headline: Interpol to aid Georgia in battle against crime.

text.p: The head of Interpol warned on Saturday that Georgia was in danger of becoming a major hub for organised crime and promised to help the small Transcaucasian nation to fight it.

Secretary-General Raymond Kendall, on a visit to Tbilisi, presided over the official opening of the international police organisation's Georgia office and met President Eduard Shevardnadze, the former Soviet foreign minister.
"The geopolitical location of Georgia makes this country ideal not only for the transit of drugs but also weapons, stolen automobiles and illegal migrants," Kendall told reporters.
Georgia, bordering Turkey, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Russia, lies at the crossroads between Europe and Asia.
The central government in the former Soviet republic has no control over 20 percent of its territory, which is in the hands of separatist groups. Its borders are regarded as porous.
Kendall said organised crime was one of the main threats to democracy in newly independent countries such as Georgia.
"Not one country can fight organised crime alone," he said, adding that Interpol would help Georgia battle "mafia-clan" infiltration of government structures.
Shevardnadze said after meeting Kendall on Friday that his country "could easily fall into the centre of attention of the criminal world".
Street crime has fallen significantly since independence from the Soviet union in 1991. But government officials say corruption and organised crime are still rife.
Shevardnadze and Interior Minister Kakha Targamadze also asked Kendall for help in exerting pressure on Russia to hand over Georgian former security minister Igor Giorgadze.

Georgia says he has been hiding in Moscow since being accused of organising a 1995 assassination attempt on Shervardnadze. The 68-year old leader escaped with cuts and bruises after a massive bomb exploded near his motorcade.
